Abstract of Thesis Parametric Evaluation of Hybrid Single-Phase Cooling Strategies for High-Heat-Flux Electronics Modern high-performance electronic systems increasingly rely on three-dimensional (3D) integration, chiplet-based packaging, and high-power artificial-intelligence accelerators, which concentrate heat generation within smaller volumes while lengthening the thermal path from interior active layers to conventional package-level cooling surfaces. These trends create localized hotspots and thermal resistances that challenge remote heat sinks and cold plates. This thesis develops and evaluates a three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer model of a hybrid single-phase cooling architecture that combines embedded microchannels with a distributed jet-impingement array. Water is used as the baseline coolant, and the model is intentionally operated at an extreme 700 W stacked-chip load to investigate the thermal-hydraulic limits of near-junction liquid cooling. A parameterized COMSOL Multiphysics model is used to evaluate microchannel mass flow rate, channel count, channel open fraction, microchannel edge margin, and jet pitch ratio/array density. Increasing channel flow and channel count reduce peak temperature but impose increasingly severe pressure-drop penalties; reducing the uncooled edge margin suppresses perimeter hotspots; and increasing open fraction produces substantial initial benefit followed by diminishing thermal returns and reduced solid wall thickness. A variable- count, fixed-total-flow jet study identifies JPR 6 as the minimum-temperature configuration, while JPR 4 provides the better balance of peak temperature, uniformity, and pressure loss. The selected configuration uses 27 microchannels per cooling layer at an open fraction of 0.80, 25 g/s microchannel flow, a 0.10 mm edge margin, and a 4 × 4 array of 300 𝜇m jets supplied by 4 g/s total jet flow. The model predicts a maximum chip temperature of approximately 374 K (101 ◦ C), a maximum thermal resistance of 0.115 K/W, and an iii

ideal total hydraulic power of 8.38 W. Relative to the baseline configuration, maximum temperature decreases by approximately 103 K and maximum thermal resistance decreases by approximately 56%. The selected design approaches the 100 ◦ C target but requires approximately 333 kPa of microchannel pressure drop, showing that hydraulic head becomes a first-order constraint once aggressive embedded cooling is used. The results demonstrate that hybrid jet-microchannel cooling should be designed as a coupled thermal, hydraulic, geometric, and packaging problem rather than as a temperature-minimization problem alone. The model provides a framework for future studies of transient hotspots, adaptive flow allocation, alternative coolants, interface reliability, and plenum-level flow distribution in next-generation 3D electronic packages. iv

Chapter 1: Introduction Three-dimensional integration, chiplet-based architectures, high-bandwidth-memory stacks, and heterogeneous packaging have become central strategies for extending electronic-system performance as conventional transistor scaling becomes more difficult and expensive. These approaches shorten electrical interconnects and increase bandwidth density, but they also concentrate power dissipation into compact packages and place active layers behind additional silicon, bonding, underfill, and interconnect interfaces. The result is a fundamental co-design problem: the same packaging technologies used to improve electrical performance can also make heat harder to remove [1]. This challenge is increasingly visible in high-performance computing and artificial-intelligence hardware, where the industry trajectory is toward greater compute density and more direct integration of cooling with the silicon and package [2], [6]. The thermal consequences are particularly severe in 3D systems. Interior heat- generating tiers have limited access to conventional external heat sinks, while localized hotspots can reach kilowatt-per-square-centimeter scales. Elevated junction temperature and large spatial thermal gradients reduce electrical efficiency, accelerate degradation of interfaces and interconnects, and constrain how densely future logic and memory can be integrated. Thermal management is therefore no longer a peripheral packaging task; it is increasingly a first-order design constraint governing attainable performance, reliability, and package architecture [1], [3]. The final 3D model in this thesis intentionally stresses this problem. A 700 W total heat load is distributed through three active tiers sharing a 5 mm × 5 mm projected footprint. On a footprint-normalized basis, this corresponds to approximately 2.8 kW/cm2 of aggregate stack power, placing the numerical study near the extreme end of demonstrated embedded-cooling research rather than at a conventional package operating point. Jet- enhanced manifold microchannels have recently demonstrated cooling at the 3,000 W/cm2 1

scale, illustrating both the relevance and severity of this operating envelope [10]. The purpose of the present loading is therefore not to reproduce a specific commercial processor, but to test whether a compact hybrid single-phase architecture can remain thermally effective as the package approaches the operational limits motivating embedded cooling. Conventional forced-air heat sinks and remote liquid cold plates remain useful at moderate heat flux, but they require heat generated inside the package to conduct through multiple layers before reaching the coolant. Single-phase microfluidic cooling offers a more direct alternative. Microchannels provide large wetted area and short conduction paths for distributed heat removal, while jet impingement can generate very high local heat- transfer coefficients through stagnation-region boundary-layer disruption [3], [7]. Neither approach is ideal by itself: straight microchannels can impose high pressure drops and streamwise temperature rise, whereas jet arrays can suffer from spatial nonuniformity, crossflow interaction, and nozzle pressure losses. Hybrid jet-microchannel systems seek to combine the localized benefit of jets with the distributed bulk transport of channels [5], [9]. The research objective is therefore to determine how a hybrid single-phase jet- 2

microchannel architecture behaves when geometric coverage, coolant allocation, temperature uniformity, and hydraulic resistance are varied together. A sequence of reduced-order, preliminary single-level, intermediate package-level, and final stacked three-dimensional COMSOL models is used to progress from basic thermal-physics verification and architecture screening to a parameterized conjugate heat-transfer model of a stacked-chip cooling architecture. The final model evaluates microchannel mass flow rate, channel count, edge margin, channel open fraction, and jet pitch ratio/array density under a 700 W steady-state load. The design is assessed using maximum and average chip temperature, temperature span, thermal resistance, pressure drop, hydraulic power, numerical conservation, and geometric feasibility. This thesis does not claim a global mathematical optimum or a complete commercial cooling loop. Instead, it identifies design trends and a selected configuration within the investigated design space, then evaluates the cost of that thermal performance in pressure head, pumping power, and remaining structural material. In this sense, the central contribution is a reproducible thermal-hydraulic modeling framework that translates the literature’s qualitative argument for embedded hybrid cooling into quantitative design guidance for extreme 3D electronic packages. 3

Chapter 2: Literature Review The literature converges on a common system-level problem: as electronic packaging moves heat generation closer together and farther from conventional cooling surfaces, the required thermal resistance decreases at the same time that pressure-drop, manufacturability, and reliability constraints become more severe. The following review therefore focuses not only on maximum heat-transfer capability, but on how microchannels, jets, hybrid architectures, and adaptive concepts redistribute the thermal and hydraulic burden within an advanced package. 2.1 Thermal Challenges in High-Heat-Flux Electronic Systems Three-dimensional integration and heterogeneous packaging increase compute density by vertically and laterally integrating logic, memory, and specialized functions. The same geometry raises thermal resistance by adding material interfaces and by locating some heat sources away from the package exterior. Reviews of microfluidic 3D-IC cooling identify embedded liquid cooling as a particularly attractive response because coolant can be placed closer to the heat-generation sites rather than relying exclusively on heat spreading to a remote surface [1]. Recent industry demonstrations similarly emphasize direct-to-silicon and near-junction microfluidics for high-power AI hardware [2], [6]. Single-phase liquid cooling is attractive because it avoids the phase-instability and vapor-management complexity of boiling systems while providing much larger heat capacity and thermal conductivity than air. Its primary penalties are hydraulic: small passages and high velocities produce pressure loss, pumping demand, and flow-distribution challenges. These tradeoffs motivate the use of geometry and flow allocation as co-equal design variables rather than treating coolant flow as an unlimited resource [3]. 4

2.2 Microchannel Heat Sinks Microchannel heat sinks remove heat through a dense network of small passages located near the heat source. Their thermal advantage arises from high surface-area-to-volume ratio, short solid conduction distances, and high convective coefficients. The microchannel literature demonstrates strong dependence on hydraulic diameter, aspect ratio, channel count, manifold design, and flow rate [3]. Straight parallel channels also exhibit three recurring limitations. First, reducing hydraulic diameter or increasing channel length can rapidly increase pressure drop. Second, coolant warms and thermal boundary layers develop along the flow direction, producing streamwise temperature nonuniformity. Third, parallel networks can suffer from mald- istribution when inlet and outlet manifolds do not distribute pressure evenly. Manifold microchannels, multilayer structures, interrupted passages, fins, and other enhancements seek to reduce these penalties, but generally increase geometric or fabrication complexity [3], [4]. 2.3 Jet Impingement Cooling Jet impingement directs coolant through one or more nozzles onto a heated surface. Near the stagnation point, momentum is redirected and the thermal boundary layer is repeatedly thinned, producing some of the highest local single-phase heat-transfer coefficients available. Jet performance depends strongly on nozzle diameter, jet Reynolds number, pitch, standoff distance, array arrangement, and crossflow environment [7], [9]. The principal limitation is spatial localization. A strong stagnation zone does not automatically produce uniform cooling across an entire die. Dense arrays increase surface coverage but can create jet interaction and crossflow, while sparse arrays place more flow through each nozzle but leave larger areas between stagnation zones. This tradeoff is especially important when total coolant flow is constrained, because jet count then changes 5

the momentum available to each nozzle. 2.4 Hybrid Jet-Microchannel Architectures Hybrid cooling combines the distributed heat-removal area of microchannels with localized boundary-layer disruption from impinging jets. Xiao et al. experimentally demonstrated a hybrid microchannel and jet-impingement heat sink with a reported thermal resistance near 0.11 K/W, illustrating the potential of the combined mechanism [5]. More recent jet-enhanced manifold microchannels extend the concept toward extremely high heat-flux operation by shortening flow paths and distributing impingement throughout the cooling structure [10]. The literature suggests that the benefit of hybridization does not come merely from adding a second cooling mechanism. Jet placement, channel geometry, total flow allocation, and pressure loss must be co-designed. A jet array that minimizes local temperature may not minimize total pumping demand, and a channel geometry that maximizes wetted area may leave insufficient wall thickness or impose excessive hydraulic head. This thesis adopts that coupled interpretation as the basis of the parametric design studies. 2.5 Adaptive and Flow-Regulated Cooling Advanced electronic workloads are spatially and temporally nonuniform, which means cooling systems designed only for the worst steady-state hotspot can waste pumping power during lower-load periods. Adaptive cooling concepts seek to redistribute coolant according to local thermal demand. Xiang et al. modeled a self-adaptive microfluidic architecture using temperature-regulated metal pillars, while Feng et al. investigated hydrogel-enhanced adaptive jet impingement using through-silicon-via concepts [4], [8]. Broader programmable- microfluidics research also demonstrates active and passive methods for changing local flow resistance and routing [11]. Adaptive flow control is not implemented in the final steady-state model developed in 6

this thesis. It remains an extension of the fixed hybrid architecture. The present study instead establishes which geometric and hydraulic parameters most strongly control temperature and pressure, providing a design basis for deciding where future adaptive control would be most useful. 2.6 Synthesis and Research Gap Table 2.1 summarizes the role of each architecture. The literature indicates that microchannels are strong distributed coolers but can become hydraulically expensive; jets provide exceptional local cooling but require careful spacing and flow allocation; hybrid architectures can combine both strengths but create a multi-objective design problem; and adaptive systems offer a mechanism for responding to nonuniform loads but add control and fabrication complexity. Chapter 3: Computational Model and Methodology The modeling strategy was developed progressively rather than beginning directly with the final three-dimensional hybrid geometry. Reduced-order and preliminary single-level models were first used to verify the expected direction of heat flow and the characteristic behavior of conventional external cooling, impinging jets, and microchannels. The final 3D model then combined these mechanisms in a parameterized conjugate heat-transfer framework. This progression reduced debugging ambiguity and provided physical context for interpreting the full model. 3.1 Modeling Progression and Validation Hierarchy 3.1.1 Reduced-Order Through-Thickness Framework A reduced-order thermal-resistance framework was used to interpret the dominant through- thickness heat-transfer mechanisms before and alongside development of the full three- dimensional conjugate model. The framework is not intended to reproduce local hotspots, lateral heat spreading, or the detailed flow distribution within the microchannels and jet chamber. Instead, it represents the stacked architecture as a one-dimensional thermal ladder in which heat conducts through the solid structure while being removed at multiple coolant interfaces. The final architecture consists of three heat-generating silicon tiers separated by two copper microchannel cooling regions, with an additional jet-impingement cooling boundary above the upper silicon tier. A purely series resistance model would therefore be inappropriate because heat is not required to travel through the complete stack before reaching a coolant sink. Instead, the two embedded microchannel layers and the upper jet-cooled surface act as parallel heat-removal branches distributed along the primary through-thickness conduction path. 3.1.4 Transition to the Final Three-Dimensional Hybrid Model The final modeling stage combined vertically stacked heat-generating domains, embedded microchannels, and an upper jet-impingement chamber into a fully three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer model. The 3D architecture was developed specifically to resolve the effects that the reduced models could not capture: lateral heat spreading, channel-to- channel coverage, corner hotspots, jet-array interaction, three-dimensional pressure loss, and the combined thermal-hydraulic consequences of varying geometric parameters. The preliminary modeling stages therefore provide a development and verification hierarchy, while the final stacked model provides the thesis’s primary quantitative results. 3.2 Final 3D Model Geometry and Heat Load The three-dimensional computational domain represents three vertically stacked, heat- generating silicon tiers. Each tier has a lateral footprint of 5 mm × 5 mm and a thickness of 100 𝜇m. The tiers are separated by solid heat-spreading regions and embedded microchannel cooling layers, producing a repeated stack in which heat is removed through internal coolant passages and an upper jet-impingement chamber. A total heat load of 700 W is distributed uniformly among the three active silicon domains, corresponding to approximately 233 W per tier. Normalized by the 5 mm × 5 mm projected footprint, the total stack load is approximately 2.8 kW/cm2 . This is intentionally an extreme steady-state condition used to evaluate the upper thermal capability of the architecture rather than to reproduce a conventional package operating point. The microchannel layers span the active chip footprint while retaining an uncut solid margin around the channel field. Channel geometry is defined by channel count, height, width, open fraction, pitch, and microchannel edge margin. In the selected configuration, 27 rectangular channels per microchannel layer are distributed across the available width. Each channel is approximately 142 𝜇m wide and 100 𝜇m high, with a pitch of approximately 179 21

𝜇m and an interchannel wall thickness of approximately 37 𝜇m. The microchannel field terminates 0.10 mm from the lateral edge of the active footprint. Above the stack, a jet plate distributes coolant through an array of circular nozzles into an impingement chamber. Jet geometry is described by nozzle diameter 𝐷 𝑗 , center-to-center jet pitch 𝑝 𝑗 , jet pitch ratio 𝑝 𝑗 /𝐷 𝑗 , and nozzle-to-surface standoff distance 𝐻. 3.10 Model Assumptions and Limitations The computational model was developed primarily for comparative evaluation of geometric and operating parameters within the proposed hybrid jet-microchannel cooling architecture. Several simplifying assumptions were therefore introduced to maintain computational feasibility while preserving the dominant thermal-fluid behavior. Water was modeled as an incompressible, single-phase liquid. Temperature- dependent water properties were obtained from the COMSOL material library, while the reduced analytical calculations used representative properties appropriate to the corre- sponding operating range. Phase change, cavitation, dissolved gases, and two-phase transport were not explicitly modeled. The validity of the single-phase assumption was evaluated for the selected config- uration by comparing the maximum coolant temperature with the saturation temperature corresponding to the local absolute pressure. The Laminar Flow interface used a reference pressure of 1 atm, such that the solved pressure field represented gauge pressure and absolute pressure was obtained from 𝑝 abs = 𝑝 + 𝑝 ref . (3.28) The resulting saturation-margin assessment is presented in Chapter 4. The applied heat load was steady and spatially uniform within each active silicon tier. Transient workload variation, moving hotspots, and transistor-level power maps were not included. The package geometry was also simplified relative to a fabricated three- dimensional integrated device. Microbumps, through-silicon vias, underfill heterogeneity, individual bonding layers, surface roughness, and thermo-mechanical deformation were not explicitly resolved unless represented by an equivalent bulk solid region. The resulting model therefore represents the thermal-fluid behavior of the proposed cooling architecture rather than a complete transistor-to-package digital twin. 36

Thermal contact resistance was not imposed as a separate interfacial boundary condition within the final three-dimensional model. The simplified solid-solid interfaces were treated using thermal continuity. Consequently, the reported selected-configuration temperatures represent an idealized bonded-interface condition and do not include the additional junction-to-coolant resistance that would be introduced by finite bond, underfill, microbump, hybrid-bond, or thermal-interface resistances in a fabricated package. Interface- resistance sensitivity and degradation are therefore treated as package-level extensions beyond the scope of the present architecture-focused study. For the final jet-array study, equal mass flow was prescribed at each nozzle inlet while total jet-branch mass flow remained fixed. This formulation provides controlled comparison of array coverage and per-jet momentum but does not resolve flow maldistribution generated by an upstream supply plenum. The earlier microchannel parameter studies used a different auxiliary jet configuration and are consequently interpreted as internally consistent sensitivity studies rather than as direct absolute comparisons with the final JPR study. All primary parameter studies were solved using the Laminar Flow interface to maintain a consistent physics formulation across the investigated design space. Reference Reynolds-number calculations show that the selected high-flow microchannel configuration extends beyond the conventional fully laminar regime. An exploratory SST turbulence-model calculation was therefore used to assess the potential model-form sensitivity of the selected configuration. The comparison is reported in Chapter 4 and is used as a sensitivity indicator rather than as a replacement for the laminar parameter-study results. Because a subsequently rebuilt SST solution with explicit reciprocal wall-distance initialization did not converge, the turbulent comparison is not treated as a fully independent validation case. Additional numerical uncertainty arises from discretization of the narrow microchan- nels, thin interchannel walls, developing flow regions, jet stagnation zones, and abrupt inlet and outlet transitions. The mesh-sensitivity study consequently considers both thermal and hydraulic quantities rather than relying exclusively on maximum temperature. These 37

assumptions and limitations permit interpretation of the parameter trends and selected design while constraining the extent to which the reported absolute values can be treated as fully validated predictions of a fabricated package. 3.11 Analytical and Numerical Validation Methods The numerical model was evaluated using complementary conservation checks, reduced-order analytical calculations, mesh sensitivity, thermodynamic consistency checks, and comparison with published experimental results. Chapter 5: Conclusions The thermal-management problem addressed by this thesis is inseparable from the packaging trajectory of modern high-performance electronics. AI accelerators, chiplet systems, high-bandwidth-memory integration, and 2.5D/3D stacking are increasing compute and interconnect density while reducing the effectiveness of remote heat-removal paths. These packaging approaches are not a short-lived exception to conventional planar design; they represent a major route by which future systems will continue to scale. As a result, cooling must increasingly move closer to the heat source and become part of package co-design rather than remain an external accessory [1], [2], [6]. This thesis developed a staged computational framework that progressed from reduced-order and preliminary single-level cooling models to a fully three-dimensional conjugate heat-transfer model of a stacked hybrid jet-microchannel architecture. The preliminary models were used to examine the expected behavior and practical limitations of conventional external cooling, jet stagnation cooling, and embedded microchannel flow before these mechanisms were combined within the final stacked configuration. The final parameterized model then evaluated the effects of channel mass flow, channel count, edge margin, open fraction, and jet pitch ratio/array density under an intentionally severe 700 W load distributed through three 5 mm × 5 mm active tiers. The parametric studies demonstrate that no single variable controls performance. Microchannel mass flow and channel count were the strongest direct levers for reducing peak temperature, but both introduced increasing hydraulic or geometric penalties. Edge margin controlled a distinct perimeter-hotspot mechanism by changing the lateral conduction distance from the chip perimeter to the cooled channel field. Open fraction produced strong benefit up to approximately 0.80 before additional thermal improvement became small relative to the loss of solid wall material. The jet-array study showed an analogous balance: JPR 6 minimized peak temperature, but JPR 4 provided the better combined result in peak 75

temperature, temperature uniformity, and pressure loss. The selected configuration combined 27 microchannels per cooling layer, an open fraction of 0.80, a 0.10 mm edge margin, 25 g/s total microchannel flow, and a 4 × 4 array of 300 𝜇m jets at JPR 4 supplied by 4 g/s total jet flow. It reduced maximum chip temperature from approximately 477 to 374 K and reduced maximum thermal resistance from 0.262 to 0.115 K/W. The design therefore approached the 100 ◦ C target under the imposed extreme load and reduced maximum thermal resistance by approximately 56% relative to the baseline. The corresponding microchannel pressure drop of approximately 333 kPa is as important as the temperature result. It demonstrates that once embedded liquid cooling is pushed toward the operating limit of a compact 3D package, the dominant design constraint can shift from insufficient heat-transfer coefficient to hydraulic head, channel geometry, and manufacturability. The selected design should therefore be understood as a high- performance thermal-hydraulic compromise within the investigated design space, not as a globally optimized or balance-of-system-ready cooling loop. The principal validation and consistency checks support the robustness of the selected thermal result while also identifying the quantities that remain more model-sensitive. In the three-level mesh study, the normal-to-fine change in maximum chip temperature was approximately 1.96%, indicating comparatively weak mesh sensitivity of the peak- temperature prediction, although pressure drop and temperature span remained more sensitive to refinement. An exploratory SST flow-model comparison similarly changed maximum chip temperature by less than 1%, while producing substantially larger changes in channel pressure drop and temperature span, indicating that the principal thermal conclusion is more robust than the absolute hydraulic and uniformity predictions. The independent rectangular-channel calculation predicted a microchannel pressure drop of approximately 324 kPa, compared with approximately 333 kPa from the numerical model, corresponding to a difference of approximately 3%. Direct integration of the COMSOL total-energy flux recovered 700.23 W from the imposed 700 W heat load, giving an energy-closure residual of only approximately 76

0.03%. Finally, the hottest coolant location remained approximately 6 K below the local saturation temperature, supporting the single-phase water assumption under the selected operating condition. Together, these checks indicate that the principal thermal conclusions are numerically and physically consistent, while hydraulic loss and detailed temperature uniformity retain greater sensitivity to modeling and discretization assumptions. The broader contribution is a reproducible framework for translating the qualitative advantages of hybrid cooling into quantitative design rules. The results support a shift toward embedded and near-junction cooling for future stacked electronics, while also showing that cooling architecture, package geometry, flow distribution, and pumping requirements must be designed together. This co-design perspective is likely to become more important as 3D integration and high-power AI hardware continue to increase internal heat density and reduce the margin available to conventional package-level thermal management. 77

Chapter 6: Future Work The present study establishes the thermal-hydraulic behavior of a parameterized hybrid microchannel and jet-impingement architecture under steady-state operating conditions. The results also identify several directions in which the architecture could be extended beyond the scope of the present work. In particular, future investigations could address realistic coolant distribution, transient and adaptive operation, package-level interface physics, alternative working fluids, expanded geometric optimization, experimental validation, and integration with the external cooling system. 6.1 Manifold and Flow-Distribution Design A natural extension of the present architecture is the explicit design of the upstream and downstream coolant-distribution systems. The jet-array study prescribed equal flow among disconnected nozzle inlets while holding total jet flow constant. This formulation isolated the influence of array density and per-jet momentum, but intentionally excluded nozzle-to-nozzle maldistribution and upstream plenum behavior. A future model incorporating a common supply plenum and return manifold could resolve these effects directly and determine whether the thermal advantages observed for the idealized jet array persist under realistic flow distribution. Manifold design is particularly important for the embedded microchannel network. The present results demonstrate that hydraulic head becomes a first-order design constraint at the flow rates required for aggressive cooling. Alternative inlet and outlet arrangements could reduce effective channel flow length, distribute coolant through additional parallel paths, or divide the chip into independently supplied cooling zones. Such architectures could potentially preserve much of the thermal performance of the selected configuration while substantially reducing pressure loss. Future optimization should therefore treat the channels, manifolds, and jet-distribution system as a coupled hydraulic network rather than 78

as independent components. 6.2 Transient and Adaptive Cooling The present work considers steady-state heat generation, whereas operating processors exhibit strongly time-dependent and spatially nonuniform power distributions. Future studies could apply transient heat maps representative of realistic computational workloads to determine the response of the hybrid architecture to moving hotspots, rapid power excursions, and spatially concentrated heat generation. Relevant performance metrics would include peak transient temperature, thermal time constant, temperature overshoot, spatial temperature gradients, and the frequency and magnitude of thermal cycling. The combination of embedded channels and localized jet cooling also provides a potential platform for adaptive thermal management. Independently controlled flow branches, microvalves, variable-pressure jet arrays, or passive temperature-responsive structures could redistribute coolant toward regions experiencing elevated heat flux. Such concepts would extend the present architecture from a fixed cooling network to a spatially responsive thermal-management system. Recent work involving programmable microfluidics and temperature-responsive or hydrogel-assisted cooling provides potential mechanisms for implementing this behavior [4], [8], [11]. 6.3 Package Interfaces and Thermomechanical Reliability The present model intentionally simplifies several package-level features in order to isolate the thermal-fluid behavior of the proposed cooling architecture. A higher-fidelity package model could incorporate thermal contact resistance, bonding layers, underfill, hybrid bonds or microbumps, through-silicon vias, and spatially varying material properties. These features introduce additional thermal resistances and heat-spreading paths that may alter both the magnitude and location of the maximum temperature. The thermal problem could also be coupled to structural mechanics to examine 79

thermomechanical reliability. Large temperature gradients across stacked tiers can generate differential thermal expansion and cyclic stresses in bonding layers and interconnects. A coupled thermal-fluid-structural model would allow cooling performance to be evaluated alongside interconnect stress, warpage, fatigue, and package lifetime. Such an analysis would be particularly valuable for determining whether aggressive localized cooling reduces mean package temperature at the expense of increased local thermal gradients or thermomechanical cycling. 6.4 Alternative Working Fluids and Two-Phase Cooling Water provides a strong single-phase thermal baseline because of its high specific heat and thermal conductivity, but it is not necessarily the preferred coolant for every implementation. Future studies could apply the same geometry and thermal-hydraulic evaluation framework to dielectric single-phase coolants, water-glycol mixtures, or other fluids selected for electrical compatibility, freeze protection, corrosion resistance, or package-material compatibility. Comparisons should consider viscosity, density, thermal conductivity, specific heat, dielectric properties, pumping requirements, material compatibility, environmental impact, and leak- management requirements in addition to temperature reduction. A more substantial extension would introduce two-phase cooling. The high local heat fluxes considered in this thesis make evaporation and flow boiling potentially attractive because latent heat transfer can provide substantial heat-removal capacity with comparatively small coolant temperature increases. Such a model would require additional treatment of nucleation, phase distribution, pressure-dependent saturation, vapor transport, flow instability, and critical heat-flux limitations. The single-phase architecture developed here could provide a geometric basis for investigating where and under what operating conditions a transition to controlled two-phase cooling becomes advantageous. 80

6.5 Expanded Geometric and Multi-Objective Optimization The parameter studies conducted in this work identify several influential design variables but sample only a discrete portion of a much larger design space. Future optimization could simultaneously vary channel width, height, aspect ratio, pitch, edge margin, flow length, nozzle diameter, nozzle shape, standoff ratio, jet spacing, and spatial jet placement. Nonuniform channel or nozzle distributions could also be designed specifically around known hotspot locations rather than using spatially uniform arrays. Such studies would benefit from a multi-objective formulation rather than optimization of maximum temperature alone. Candidate objective functions could include maximum temperature, temperature nonuniformity, pressure drop, pumping power, coolant flow rate, and package volume. Manufacturability could be incorporated through constraints on minimum wall thickness, channel aspect ratio, lithographic or etching tolerances, sealing requirements, pressure containment, and assembly processes. The resulting Pareto space would provide a more useful design tool than a single temperature-minimizing configuration by explicitly quantifying the cost of additional thermal performance. 6.6 Experimental Demonstration and Validation Experimental investigation represents an important next step beyond the computational framework developed in this thesis. A representative test article containing embedded microchannels and a jet-cooled surface could be used to measure pressure loss, coolant temperature rise, surface temperature distribution, and overall thermal resistance under controlled heat loads. These measurements would provide direct validation of the conjugate heat-transfer predictions and could quantify effects that are difficult to represent numerically, including surface roughness, manufacturing tolerances, leakage, imperfect bonding, flow maldistribution, and contact resistance. A staged experimental program could begin with individual microchannel and 81

jet-impingement test structures before progressing to a stacked hybrid assembly. Such an approach would allow the hydraulic and thermal behavior of each cooling mechanism to be characterized independently before their interaction is examined in the complete architecture. Experimental data could subsequently support refinement of turbulence, conjugate heat-transfer, and package-interface models for increasingly realistic stacked devices. 6.7 Chip-to-System Thermal Co-Design Finally, the proposed architecture could be extended from a chip-scale thermal-management concept to a complete cooling-system model. The present work demonstrates that high thermal performance can coexist with substantial hydraulic-head requirements, making the interaction between the embedded coolant network and the external loop an important system- level problem. Future models could couple the chip-scale pressure-flow characteristics to pump performance, tubing, valves, manifolds, heat exchangers, and facility cooling infrastructure. This extension would permit optimization based on total system performance rather than chip temperature alone. Metrics such as pump electrical power, heat-rejection temperature, cooling-system coefficient of performance, coolant inventory, package volume, and facility-level energy consumption could be considered alongside junction temperature and thermal resistance. Ultimately, such an approach would treat the cooling architecture, electronic package, and external thermal infrastructure as a coupled design problem. This system-level perspective represents a logical progression from the hybrid near-junction cooling architecture investigated in the present work toward practical implementation in future high-power 2.5D and 3D electronic systems. 82
